scope: Factual energy/state correction and one intrinsic prerequisite correction; no new topic, source context, age, activity deletion or learner-state operation.

cardCorrections.before: Explain that heating adds energy causing particles to move more, leading to state changes
cardCorrections.after: Explain that heating transfers energy: warming within a state can increase particle motion, while melting at a constant temperature changes particle arrangement/interactions without requiring faster motion.
cardCorrections.reason: Retain qualitative energy/particle explanation, correcting the false implication that motion must speed up during a melting plateau.

guideCorrections.before:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Heating & Cooling Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'States of matter'):** Pupils should be taught to "observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)." Non-statutory guidance: "note the changes to water when it is heated or cooled"; research melting/condensing temperatures (e.g. when iron melts, when oxygen condenses); explore the effect of temperature on chocolate, butter, cream. Note: teachers should AVOID materials where heating causes chemical change (baking, burning).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-4):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." Clarification: reversible examples include water and butter at different temperatures. DCI PS1.B: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence.

- **Operational details:** Establish the two reversible state changes for water — melting (solid→liquid) and freezing (liquid→solid) — plus boiling/evaporation, and tie each to a MEASURED temperature: water freezes/melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C. Have children read a thermometer in °C and record the temperature at which a change happens, so the abstract change is pinned to a number. Use gentle everyday examples (chocolate, butter, ice) and explicitly keep to physical, reversible changes, avoiding burning/cooking. Confront the melting–dissolving confusion head-on (ice melting is heat-driven state change; sugar dissolving is a different process). The particle-level 'why' (heating gives particles more energy to move) is a light bridge to KS3, not the KS2 core, which is observe-and-measure.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (observational→early-quantitative). The child can describe melting and freezing with everyday examples, state that water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C, read a thermometer in °C to record where a change occurs, and keep melting distinct from dissolving.
guideCorrections.after:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Heating & Cooling Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'States of matter'):** Pupils should be taught to "observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens in degrees Celsius (°C)." Non-statutory guidance: "note the changes to water when it is heated or cooled"; research melting/condensing temperatures (e.g. when iron melts, when oxygen condenses); explore the effect of temperature on chocolate, butter, cream. Note: teachers should AVOID materials where heating causes chemical change (baking, burning).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-4):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." Clarification: reversible examples include water and butter at different temperatures. DCI PS1.B: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-4]." SEP: Engaging in Argument from Evidence.

- **Operational details:** Establish the two reversible state changes for water — melting (solid→liquid) and freezing (liquid→solid) — plus boiling/evaporation, and anchor changes to a safely measured or reliably researched temperature: water freezes/melts at 0°C and boils at 100°C. Retain an actual safe thermometer reading in °C as part of the whole shared claim; boiling and extreme-temperature values can be researched without child hot-water handling. Use gentle everyday examples (chocolate, butter, ice) and explicitly keep to physical, reversible changes, avoiding burning/cooking. Confront the melting–dissolving confusion head-on (ice melting is heat-driven state change; sugar dissolving is a different process). The national KS2 minimum centres on observation/measurement. This whole shared claim also retains its qualitative energy/particle evidence: warming within a state can increase motion, whereas constant-temperature melting changes arrangement/interactions without requiring faster motion. Full independent three-state dot-diagram construction is supporting work, not a necessary prerequisite.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (observational→early-quantitative). The child can describe melting and freezing with everyday examples, state that water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C, read a thermometer in °C to record where a change occurs, and keep melting distinct from dissolving.
guideCorrections.reason: Separate national minimum from the complete shared claim; retain actual measurement and qualitative explanation without unsafe boiling or plateau error.

guideCorrections.before: Pin every state change to a MEASURED temperature in °C (water: 0°C freeze/melt, 100°C boil), so children read and record, not just watch.
guideCorrections.after: Anchor state changes to a measured or reliably researched temperature in °C (pure water at normal atmospheric pressure: freeze/melt0°C, boil100°C). Include an actual safe thermometer reading/recording task in the whole shared claim; boiling and extreme-temperature values are research examples, not child handling.
guideCorrections.reason: Preserve numeric/measurement demands while not requiring literal measurement of every extreme/boiling example.

guideCorrections.before: For ages 7–9: observe that some materials change state when heated or cooled, and pin each change to a MEASURED temperature in °C (pure water melts/freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure). Core skill is observe-and-measure: read a thermometer and record the temperature where a change happens. Some mixtures, such as chocolate, soften and melt over a range of temperatures rather than at one sharp point. Keep melting distinct from dissolving, keep to physical reversible changes (avoid burning/cooking), and show that melting and freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. Particle-level 'why' is a light bridge, not the core.
guideCorrections.after: For ages 7–9: observe that some materials change state when heated or cooled, and anchor changes to safely measured or reliably researched temperatures in °C (pure water melts/freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure). Core skill is observe-and-measure: read a thermometer and record the temperature where a change happens. Some mixtures, such as chocolate, soften and melt over a range of temperatures rather than at one sharp point. Keep melting distinct from dissolving, keep to physical reversible changes (avoid burning/cooking), and show that melting and freezing are the same boundary crossed in opposite directions. The national minimum need not require a full particle model, but the complete shared claim still includes a correct qualitative energy/particle explanation: within-state warming can increase motion; constant-temperature melting changes arrangement/interactions without a required speed increase.

guideCorrections.before: It's the same water — melting is a change of STATE (solid to liquid), not a change into a new material; cooling reverses it back to ice. Ice melts at 0°C and water boils at 100°C. Heating adds energy so the particles move more and the solid becomes liquid.
guideCorrections.after: It's the same water — melting is a change of STATE (solid to liquid), not a change into a new material; cooling reverses it back to ice. Ice melts at 0°C and water boils at 100°C. Heating transfers energy. Within-state warming can increase particle motion; during a constant-temperature melting plateau the energy changes particle arrangement/interactions without requiring faster motion.
guideCorrections.reason: Correct the actual expected answer while retaining qualitative energy reasoning.

guideCorrections.before: Explains melting, freezing and boiling as reversible changes of state of the SAME material at fixed temperatures, driven by adding or removing heat energy, and distinguishes melting from dissolving.
guideCorrections.after: Explains melting, freezing and boiling as reversible changes of state of the SAME material at fixed temperatures, driven by adding or removing heat energy, and distinguishes melting from dissolving. Gives the required qualitative energy/particle explanation without asserting a speed increase during a constant-temperature plateau.
guideCorrections.reason: Keep whole shared energy evidence visible in the rubric, not silently treated as optional.

guideCorrections.before: Model melting: take the solid and show its particles loosening out of the regular pattern into a disordered arrangement and speeding up — staying close together (still touching, not moving far apart; only a small spacing change) and remaining the same particles — then annotate what changed.
guideCorrections.after: Model melting: take the solid and show its particles loosening out of the regular pattern into a disordered arrangement without requiring a speed increase during constant-temperature melting — staying close together (still touching, not moving far apart; only a small spacing change) and remaining the same particles — then annotate what changed.
guideCorrections.reason: Correct the actual manipulation instruction, preserving same particles/close spacing and arrangement change.

guideCorrections.before: A particle diagram becomes a working model only when it both shows arrangement and moves: from it a learner can explain why solids keep shape, liquids flow, and gases can be squashed, and why heating to melt rearranges and speeds up particles without changing the particles themselves.
guideCorrections.after: A particle diagram becomes a working model only when it both shows arrangement and moves: from it a learner can explain why solids keep shape, liquids flow, and gases can be squashed, and why melting rearranges the same particles while their average motion need not increase during a constant-temperature plateau.

guideCorrections.before: On the melting question, confirm: the dots stay the same size and number, while the regular pattern becomes disordered and the particles speed up, with only a small change in spacing — they do not fly far apart (that would be becoming a gas).
guideCorrections.after: On the melting question, confirm: the dots stay the same size and number, while the regular pattern becomes disordered without requiring the particles to speed up during a constant-temperature plateau, with only a small change in spacing — they do not fly far apart (that would be becoming a gas).
guideCorrections.reason: Correct the direct feedback on the melting answer.

guideCorrections.before: Melting (solid→liquid) keeps particles close/touching while changing a regular pattern to a disordered one and speeding them up, with only a small spacing change; do not depict particles moving far apart on melting (that depicts becoming a gas).
guideCorrections.after: Melting (solid→liquid) keeps particles close/touching while changing a regular pattern to a disordered one without requiring a speed increase during constant-temperature melting, with only a small spacing change; do not depict particles moving far apart on melting (that depicts becoming a gas).
guideCorrections.reason: Correct the repeated constraint without changing any other diagram criterion.

primaryFactualSupport.title: University Physics Volume2 §1.5 Phase Changes
primaryFactualSupport.actuallyRead: Actual publisher body: phase diagrams/pressure assumptions, equilibrium, Phase Change and Latent Heat, heating-curve Figure1.15 and microscopic explanation at extracted lines70–97. No videos viewed.
primaryFactualSupport.boundedFact: Pure-water melting at ordinary constant pressure can absorb energy while temperature stays at the transition value; energy changes intermolecular interactions/arrangement without requiring greater average kinetic motion. Warming within a state and changing state are different energy pathways.
primaryFactualSupport.useLimit: Factual accuracy support only, not primary-age pedagogy/efficacy proof; no textbook figure, exercise, quotation or licensed activity is redistributed.

primaryFactualSupport.title: David Bauer, UCLA Physics5B Chapter2 Specific Heat and Phase Changes
primaryFactualSupport.actuallyRead: Complete lecture main body, including specific heat, phase-change sections and heating-curve explanation
primaryFactualSupport.boundedFact: Heating curves distinguish sloping single-phase temperature changes from latent-heat plateaus.
primaryFactualSupport.useLimit: Independent university factual corroboration, not advanced formula/clinical gate or child age proof. Intermolecular interactions are not chemical transformation of the particles.

originalDiagnosticCases.given: Pure water ice warms from below0°C to its melting point at normal atmospheric pressure.
Both ice and liquid water remain while energy enters the sample at its normal-pressure melting point.
All ice has melted; additional energy warms liquid water within its liquid range at normal pressure.

wholeClaimWitness.observedStateChanges: Actually observe a safe adult-prepared melting ice/water sample and identify reversible solid→liquid and liquid→solid cases. Distinguish melting from a solid dispersing/dissolving in a second liquid.
wholeClaimWitness.actualMeasurement: Read a suitable Celsius thermometer during the ice/water observation, record near0°C while both phases remain, and distinguish later warming after all ice is gone. Ordinary pressure/pure-water reference0/100 is supplied/taught; boiling is researched/prepared evidence, never a child hot-water task.
wholeClaimWitness.qualitativeExplanation: Explain that adding/removing energy can change state; warming within a state can increase particle motion, while energy during isothermal melting changes arrangement/state rather than requiring a temperature or speed rise. The same material can return on cooling.
wholeClaimWitness.changedCase: Use a material-specific butter/reference case and non-transition warming-water case; do not assert every warmed object melts or all mixtures have a single sharp melting point.
wholeClaimWitness.independentMissingPrerequisite: The same learner may be unable to independently generate all solid/liquid/gas dot diagrams, annotate gas motion/empty gaps and explain compressibility. Nothing in complete Heating description/evidence/assessment requires that representational inventory.

compatibility: Real evidence/rubric clarification: retain the prior claim/research revision downstream. No automatic equivalence, transfer, reset or publication is authorised.
